attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, presenting AWS figures he reports himself.

semantics.note: Captures the June jump and the 'never returned' claim, bounded at September, which matches the post's data range. It leaves out the hedged 'I believe' minority aside, which is fine because that part is hedged and not scored.

contract.note: Reading 'that same month' as June vs May and 'previous levels' as May's bill is the ordinary reading. Treating 104% as approximate is fair. Keeping the hedged minority aside as a separate component is reasonable.

evidence.note: Cursor's own pricing post about rising per-request token costs. It gives no AWS invoice figures for May–September 2025.

reviews.rationale: The claim depends on Cursor's monthly AWS bills, and only Zitron reports them. His figures are internally consistent (12.67 vs 6.19 is about +104%, and July–September all stay above May), but that only checks his arithmetic. The packet has no independent invoices or disclosures, so it does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own conjecture in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I'd be shocked if it was anything less' is a high-confidence commitment, not a 'very likely' probability. Recording it as 'likely' downgrades it to a hedge. The 'real trouble' consequence is kept as a conditional but has no measurable threshold.

contract.note: Scoring the January–September 2025 ratio of Google Cloud to AWS spend against 0.5 follows from the surrounding calculation. Treating 'real trouble' as qualitative and unscored is fair.

evidence.note: Anthropic's October 2025 announcement of a planned Google expansion. It is forward-looking and after the target period, and gives no historical spend or AWS ratio.

reviews.rationale: The ratio claim is firm enough to score, but the packet has no same-period Google Cloud and AWS spending figures. The only item is a later, forward-looking capacity announcement, which cannot establish what was spent January–September 2025. The 'real trouble' consequence has no threshold and its condition is unverified.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analysis in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'appear' and the estimated-revenue basis. The 'likely' modality label overstates the hedge a little, since 'appear' qualifies an observed pattern. The pricing conclusion is a firm inference drawn from it.

contract.note: January–September 2025, roughly proportional growth, and revenue failing to cover costs is a fair ordinary reading. Assessing the two components separately is appropriate.

evidence.note: Company run-rate figures (about $1B at the start of 2025, over $5B by August). These are annualized, not realized monthly revenue, and there are no matching AWS charges.

reviews.rationale: Neither part can be tested from the packet. It has no independent monthly AWS spending and no realized revenue or full-cost series for January–September 2025, only annualized run-rate milestones. So it cannot show whether AWS costs tracked revenue near-linearly, or whether pricing failed to cover costs.

attribution.note: Zitron's own argument in his own post.

semantics.note: Both hypothetical branches keep their antecedents. The 'will' label is not in the text: the success branch's consequence is a present-tense assertion ('clearly unprofitable revenue'), and the demise branch is close to a truism.

contract.note: Calling the success branch met depends on the evaluator reading 'lets Cursor succeed' as continued commercial scale. Zitron did not define success. 'Unprofitable' has no stated cost-allocation basis.

evidence.note: Cursor's own disclosure of passing $1B annualized revenue. It bears on the success condition only, not on Anthropic's margin from Cursor.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's reading the success condition is plausibly met, but the packet has no customer-level data on Anthropic's revenue and costs for Cursor, so 'clearly unprofitable' cannot be checked. The demise branch's condition did not occur. No deadline was stated.
